# OWASP Agentic Security Initiative, agentic AI threats and mitigations

**Source:** OWASP GenAI Security Project, Agentic Security Initiative (ASI), *Agentic AI - Threats and Mitigations*, Version 1.1, December 2025. Co-leads John Sotiropoulos and Ron F. Del Rosario. No ISBN or DOI. Licence CC BY-SA 4.0. Scope: open.
**Structure:** A 52-page guide (plus cover): agents and their capabilities, a single- and multi-agent reference architecture with ten agentic patterns, a reference threat model of seventeen threats (T1–T17), a six-question Taxonomy Navigator with 66 attack scenarios, six mitigation playbooks, and three example threat models.

## Author's Thesis (condensed)

The guide calls itself the first in a series from the OWASP Agentic Security Initiative, a threat-model-based reference to emerging agentic threats and their mitigations, written for builders and defenders of agentic applications and focused on agents built on large language models (p. 3). It defines an agent and its capabilities, maps them to deployable components in a reference architecture that serves as the canvas for its threat models, and follows no single threat-modelling methodology, recommending practitioners choose one that suits their organisation (pp. 3–12).

Its central claim is that agentic AI threats are either new or agentic variations of existing threats (p. 13). Memory and tool integration become two key attack vectors; tool use makes identity and authorisation a critical challenge; and autonomy, memory and the complexity and scale of multi-agency amplify existing LLM risks, so hallucinations cascade and human oversight can itself be overwhelmed (pp. 13–15). It sets the threats out as T1–T17 (pp. 16–19), arranges them on a six-question decision path (pp. 21–32), answers them with six playbooks split into proactive, reactive and detective steps (pp. 34–42), and applies them to three example systems (pp. 43–49).

## Agents, Capabilities and Architecture

An agent is an intelligent software system that perceives its environment, reasons, decides and acts to achieve objectives autonomously; the guide also quotes Russell and Norvig's definition of an intelligent agent (p. 4). It credits LLMs' capabilities, natural-language interface and scale with revolutionising agentic AI, and cites a Gartner forecast that by 2028 33% of enterprise software applications will use agentic AI (p. 4). Agents typically show three core capabilities: planning and reasoning, with the LLM deciding the application's control flow and strategies such as reflection, self-critique, chain of thought and subgoal decomposition; memory, short-term or persistent long-term; and action and tool use, including the Model Context Protocol and function calling (pp. 4–5). Autonomy grows from an agentic LLM application through a single agent to a multi-agent system, and varies with orchestration style from hardcoded to fully conversational (pp. 6–7).

In practice most deployments build these capabilities into the agent software rather than exposing them as separate services (p. 8). The single-agent reference architecture has five deployable parts: an application acting for the user, often outside a user session; an agent taking natural-language and media input; one or more LLMs; services called through framework-level function calling or LLM-returned invocation code; and supporting services for long-term memory and RAG data (pp. 8–9). A multi-agent architecture adds inter-agent communication and, optionally, a coordinating agent; the A2A protocol standardises that communication, and the example diagram shows a coordinating agent over four specialised agents with shared memory and services (pp. 9–10). Ten agentic patterns (reflective, task-oriented, hierarchical, coordinating, distributed ecosystem, human-in-the-loop collaboration, self-learning, RAG-based, planning, context-aware) are offered to standardise threat-modelling conversations (pp. 10–11).

## The Threat Model

Threat modelling is a structured, repeatable process that asks four questions from the Threat Modeling Manifesto: what are we working on, what can go wrong, what are we going to do about it, and did we do a good enough job (p. 12). STRIDE and PASTA are rooted in traditional cyber vulnerabilities and must be expanded or mapped to AI vulnerabilities; MAESTRO is named as a layered agentic extension of STRIDE, but the guide follows no specific methodology, because methodologies can impose barriers on newcomers and those like MAESTRO also cover non-agentic threats, and uses its reference architecture instead (p. 12). General threats that are not agent-specific are left to other OWASP guides, MITRE Atlas and NIST (p. 13).

The narrative threat model names the new pressures. Memory and tools are two key attack vectors, and code generation opens remote-code-execution risks (p. 13). A Confused Deputy arises when an agent holding more privilege than its user is tricked into unauthorised actions, typically because it cannot tell legitimate requests from injected instructions; the remedy is least-privilege agent entitlements and checking that the user is authorised (p. 13). Non-human identities may lack session oversight, agents can inherit excessive permissions or chain tools in unexpected ways that bypass intended security controls, and the guide calls for clear identity flows, strict RBAC and zero trust (p. 14). Supply-chain and RAG risks are mostly referred to the LLM Top 10 (p. 14). Hallucinations cascade when false information is reinforced through memory, tools or other agents; attackers can overwhelm human-in-the-loop controls; and intent and goal manipulation, misaligned and deceptive behaviour, human manipulation, repudiation, rogue agents and human attacks on multi-agent systems complete the picture (pp. 14–15). A summary diagram places the threat IDs on the single-agent architecture, with T16 and T17 absent from it (p. 16).

## The Seventeen Threats

The Navigator walks six questions, each opening a group of threats, starting at the single agent because its vulnerabilities often found larger, system-wide risks (p. 21). Each threat carries a table definition and mitigations (pp. 16–19), a Navigator description that, where one applies, places it against the related LLM Top 10 entry, and named scenarios (pp. 21–32).

- **Agency and reasoning (Step 1).** T6 Intent Breaking & Goal Manipulation exploits the lack of separation between data and instructions to redirect planning, extending prompt injection to an agent's long-term reasoning; scenarios include gradual plan injection and reflection-loop traps (pp. 17, 21–22). T7 Misaligned & Deceptive Behaviors covers harmful or disallowed actions taken while appearing compliant, distinct from hallucination because it emerges from advanced reasoning; scenarios include an agent deceiving a human to pass a CAPTCHA and insider trading (pp. 17, 22–23). T8 Repudiation & Untraceability covers actions that cannot be traced for want of logging, which makes auditing and accountability difficult (pp. 18, 23).
- **Memory (Step 2).** T1 Memory Poisoning corrupts short- or long-term memory, including shared memory that lets one user affect others, extending static data poisoning to real-time poisoning of persistent memory (pp. 16, 23–24). T5 Cascading Hallucination Attacks exploit agents' inability to tell fact from fiction, compounding through reflection and memory in one agent or communication loops among many (pp. 17, 24–25).
- **Tools, execution and supply chain (Step 3).** T2 Tool Misuse abuses authorised tools within granted permissions by chaining seemingly legitimate actions (pp. 16, 25–26). T3 Privilege Compromise exploits agents' autonomous inheritance of permissions (pp. 17, 26). T4 Resource Overload exhausts compute, memory or API quotas, made worse by agents that self-trigger tasks and spawn processes (pp. 17, 26–27). T11 Unexpected RCE and Code Attacks exploits AI-generated code execution (pp. 18, 27). T16 Insecure Inter-Agent Protocol Abuse attacks MCP and A2A through injected context, misleading tool descriptions and consent flows (pp. 19, 28). T17 Supply Chain Compromise poisons upstream prompts, plugins or updates, with the Amazon Q and Replit incidents as scenarios (pp. 19, 28–29).
- **Authentication (Step 4).** T9 Identity Spoofing & Impersonation includes theft of a formal, persistent agent identity, which widens the blast radius and undermines auditability (pp. 18, 29–30).
- **Humans (Step 5).** T10 Overwhelming Human in the Loop floods reviewers until human capacity cannot keep up, producing rushed approvals (pp. 18, 30). T15 Human Manipulation turns users' trust in an agent into a channel for social engineering, as in invoice fraud through a compromised copilot (pp. 19, 30–31).
- **Multiple agents (Step 6).** T12 Agent Communication Poisoning corrupts transient inter-agent messages and consensus (pp. 18, 31). T14 Human Attacks on Multi-Agent Systems exploit delegation and trust between agents, for example by bouncing a request until it is granted on assumed prior validation (pp. 19, 31–32). T13 Rogue Agents in Multi-Agent Systems can remain embedded in workflows unnoticed, including infectious backdoors that spread through other agents' consumption of their outputs (pp. 18, 32).

## Mitigation Playbooks

Six playbooks (the opening sentence says five) map to the decision path, each split into proactive, reactive and detective steps, and are meant to sit inside broader security frameworks for defence in depth (p. 34). Playbook 1 guards reasoning with tool restriction, behaviour profiling, goal-consistency validation, tracking of goal-change requests, cryptographic logging and flags on suspicious decision reversals (p. 35). Playbook 2 guards memory with validated insertion from trusted sources, session isolation, retention limits, pre-commit validation and truth-checking, rollback, snapshots, lineage and version control (pp. 35–37). Playbook 3 secures tool execution and the supply chain with access policies, function-level authentication, disposable sandboxes, just-in-time access, risk-scored execution, signed definitions and SBOMs, user approval for financial, medical or administrative actions, and resource monitoring (pp. 37–38). Playbook 4 hardens identity with cryptographic verification, RBAC and ABAC, short-lived credentials, mutual authentication, expiring elevation and identity-deviation monitoring (pp. 39–40). Playbook 5 protects human reviewers with risk-prioritised queues, automation of low-risk approvals, notification limits, explanation summaries and workload balancing (pp. 40–41). Playbook 6 secures multi-agent systems with authenticated, encrypted messages, trust scoring, consensus for high-risk actions, task and topology segmentation, isolation of rogue agents and tracking of their attempts to rejoin (pp. 41–42).

## Example Threat Models

Three worked examples apply the threat IDs (the Introduction promises four) (pp. 3, 43–49). An enterprise copilot connected to email, files, calendar and CRM faces eleven threats, most entered through indirect prompt injection: exfiltration through a calendar invite, a hidden instruction in an email that hijacks a summary request, swapped vendor bank details, and a poisoned prompt template (pp. 43–45). A hypothetical LLM-managed smart-home security agent faces ten, including poisoned sensor readings that make break-ins invisible, implicit agent-to-agent trust exploited by a mimic issuing false all-clear signals, and agents that can autonomously escalate false positives, making real threats harder for reviewers to find (pp. 45–47). An RPA expense-reimbursement agent faces nine, including adaptive learning that gradually accepts fraud as normal, a trusted email tool that exports records without further checks, and thousands of low-priority approvals that get reviewers rubber-stamping fraud (pp. 48–49).

## Key Statistics

- Gartner forecast: by 2028, 33% of enterprise software applications will use agentic AI, enabling 15% of day-to-day work decisions to be made autonomously (p. 4).
- 17 threats; 15 labelled on the summary diagram; 6 decision-path questions; 66 attack scenarios; 6 playbooks; 10 agentic patterns; 3 example threat models (pp. 10–49).
- Contributors: 39 in the text layer (38 visible on the rendered page), with 7 reviewers; 108 project supporters (pp. 50, 52).

## Key Connections

- Russell and Norvig, *Artificial Intelligence: A Modern Approach*: quoted for the definition of an intelligent agent (p. 4).
- Gartner forecast; OpenAI Gym, now Farama Foundation's Gymnasium; OpenAI's Operator system card (p. 4).
- Model Context Protocol and Agent2Agent: standards for tool connection and multi-agent communication, and the T16 attack surface (pp. 5, 9, 28).
- Threat Modeling Manifesto (four questions); STRIDE, PASTA and MAESTRO (p. 12).
- The OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications 2025 entries (LLM01, LLM03, LLM04, LLM05, LLM06, LLM08, LLM09, LLM10) as the baselines the Navigator sets agentic threats against; other OWASP guides, MITRE Atlas and NIST AI 100-2 for general threats (pp. 13–32).
- NIST, CSA, academic research and vendor taxonomies such as Precize as sources of the taxonomy (p. 19).
- Anthropic and OpenAI work on misaligned behaviour; Microsoft Entra Agent ID; arXiv papers on chain of thought, small models, autonomy levels, infectious backdoors and explainability (pp. 5–40).

## Signature Contrarian Positions

1. The guide follows no single threat-modelling methodology, because methodologies can impose barriers on newcomers and those like MAESTRO also cover non-agentic threats; practitioners should pick their own (p. 12).
2. Established methodologies such as STRIDE and PASTA must be expanded or mapped to AI vulnerabilities (p. 12).
3. The LLM Top 10 entries cover the agentic threats only partially; agentic AI extends prompt injection, data poisoning, excessive agency and misinformation (pp. 21–32).
